proposal.reason: Trial 1 word C=0.3 has macro_f1 0.498 and spam recall 0.030, indicating a severe ham-only bias. Switching to char n-grams with C=3.0 tests a different feature space and less regularization that may capture spam-specific substrings missed by word tokens; no improvement is assumed.
proposal.review: Trial 1 is the only completed primary-split evidence. Its high ham recall and near-zero spam recall make minority-class recall the main observed failure, but this does not prove any candidate will fix it.
proposal.hypothesis: Char n-gram features with C=3.0 may capture spam-specific substrings and reduce the ham-only bias seen in trial 1, potentially raising macro_f1.
proposal.uncertainty: Only one completed primary trial; no confirmation split. Char features and higher C may overfit or still miss spam; direction and magnitude of macro_f1 change are unknown.

proposal.reason: Trial 2 (char C=3.0) is the best completed primary result with macro_f1 0.9439 and spam recall 0.8182, while trial 1 (word C=0.3) had severe ham-only bias with spam recall 0.0303. A word+char representation at C=3.0 tests whether adding word-token features to the successful char feature space captures complementary cues.
proposal.review: Only two primary trials are available, and trial 1 changed both representation and C relative to trial 2, so the cause of trial 2's improvement is not isolated. There is no confirmation-split evidence and no direct evidence for word+char features; the combination may add noise as well as signal.
proposal.hypothesis: Word+char features with C=3.0 may combine char-substring and word-token signals and potentially improve macro_f1 or spam recall, but no improvement is assumed and the direction is unknown.
proposal.uncertainty: No direct word+char evidence exists. Only primary-split results are available, with no confirmation split. Trial 1 and trial 2 differ in both representation and C, so effects are not isolated. The combined representation may overfit or add noise; macro_f1 change is unknown.
